column2: An agreement enforceable by law
column3: An agreement must satisfy legal enforceability requirements to be a contract.
column4: Every social agreement is automatically an enforceable contract.

column2: A proposal intended to obtain assent to specified terms
column3: A definite proposal communicated to the offeree differs from a general invitation to negotiate.
column4: Every displayed advertisement is automatically a binding offer regardless of its wording and context.

column2: An invitation for others to submit offers rather than a definite offer itself
column3: A routine goods display with price labels generally invites the buyer's offer, subject to the transaction's actual circumstances.
column4: Every ordinary shop display legally guarantees acceptance of every customer's purchase proposal.

column2: Assent to an offer's terms under the applicable requirements
column3: Changing an offered price while claiming to accept ordinarily creates a counteroffer rather than unqualified acceptance.
column4: Changing the offered price always constitutes absolute and unqualified acceptance.

column2: Something of value given promised or done at the promisor's desire
column3: Under Indian contract law, consideration may move from the promisee or another person, subject to other enforceability rules.
column4: Consideration under Indian law can move only from the promisee in every case.

column2: An act already done at the promisor's desire capable of qualifying as consideration
column3: Under Indian law, a prior act done at the promisor's desire is distinguished from an unsolicited past act.
column4: Every unsolicited prior favour is automatically valid contractual consideration for every later promise.

column2: The general rule that contractual enforcement belongs to parties subject to recognised exceptions
column3: The rule on who may provide consideration is distinct from the general rule on who can sue under the contract.
column4: Because consideration can come from another person, every stranger can automatically sue on every contract.

column2: Legal competence to enter an enforceable contract
column3: Competence requires relevant age soundness of mind and absence of legal disqualification.
column4: Possessing a large bank balance alone proves contractual competence regardless of age and mental capacity.

column2: An agreement involving a person below the relevant age of majority
column3: A minor's agreement is generally void from the beginning; necessary supplies can raise a distinct reimbursement claim against the minor's property.
column4: Providing necessaries creates an ordinary personal contractual liability against the minor exactly like an adult debtor.

column2: Ability to understand a contract and form rational judgment about its effect at the relevant time
column3: A normally unsound person may contract during a lucid interval when the statutory competence conditions are met.
column4: A person ever experiencing unsoundness can never contract during a lucid interval.

column2: Consent not caused by specified vitiating factors
column3: Consent induced by coercion is distinguished from consent freely given merely because the agreement is written.
column4: A signed written agreement automatically rules out coercion and undue influence.

column2: Consent obtained through statutorily specified unlawful threats or acts
column3: Threatening unlawful detention of property to procure agreement can involve coercion.
column4: Coercion can arise only from physical injury already inflicted on the contracting person.

column2: Improper use of a position dominating another's will to obtain unfair advantage
column3: A relationship of domination and unfair advantage can matter even without physical threats.
column4: Without a physical threat, undue influence is legally impossible in every relationship.

column2: Intentional deceptive conduct within the relevant statutory definition
column3: An intentional false material representation differs from an innocent mistaken statement.
column4: Every innocent mistake is automatically intentional fraud.

column2: A misleading statement within the statutory definition without the necessary fraudulent intent
column3: A false representation may affect consent even when intentional deception is not established.
column4: A representation cannot affect contractual consent unless criminal fraud is proved.

column2: A shared essential factual mistake that can make an agreement void
column3: A mistake about an essential existing fact differs from a unilateral error about the bargain's desirability.
column4: Every unilateral regret about price automatically voids the contract as a bilateral mistake.

column2: An agreement lacking legal enforceability
column3: An agreement can be void without necessarily constituting a criminal offence.
column4: Every void agreement is necessarily a criminal act.

column2: A contract enforceable at the option of the party entitled to avoid it
column3: A contract induced by a qualifying consent defect can be avoided by the affected party under applicable conditions.
column4: The wrongdoer alone necessarily holds the option to avoid every contract induced by that wrongdoer's coercion.

column2: A contract purpose that meets statutory legality requirements
column3: A bargain to perform an unlawful act cannot be rescued simply by offering a higher price.
column4: Adequate consideration makes an unlawful contractual object lawful.

column2: A restriction on lawful trade assessed under statutory rules and exceptions
column3: Indian law's general rule of voidness in restraint of trade must be read with recognised statutory exceptions, such as qualified goodwill-sale restraints.
column4: Every conceivable restraint of trade is valid whenever one party calls it commercially convenient.

column2: A contract dependent on a collateral uncertain event
column3: A contractual obligation triggered by a specified uncertain collateral event differs from an unconditional promise.
column4: A contingent contract is unconditional merely because the promised amount is definite.

column2: An agreement for gain or loss on an uncertain event with the relevant wagering features
column3: A wager differs from insurance supported by insurable interest and legitimate risk protection.
column4: Every valid insurance contract is necessarily a wager solely because payment depends on an uncertain event.

column2: Carrying out contractual obligations as required
column3: Proper performance discharges the relevant obligation, while part performance may leave remaining obligations.
column4: Any partial performance automatically discharges every remaining contractual duty.

column2: Substitution of a new contract for an existing one by agreement
column3: A valid agreed substitution can discharge the old contract rather than merely add another identical promise.
column4: Novation always requires keeping every old obligation enforceable without change.

column2: The promisee's acceptance of less or dispensing with performance under the applicable rule
column3: Under the Indian Contract Act, a promisee may remit performance without the same consideration requirement as an ordinary fresh bargain.
column4: A promisee can never remit any part of a contractual obligation without receiving additional money.

column2: Discharge when a subsequent event makes performance impossible or unlawful under the rule
column3: A mere fall in profitability is not automatically legal impossibility.
column4: Any reduction in expected profit necessarily frustrates the contract.

column2: Repudiation before performance becomes due
column3: A clear pre-due-date refusal to perform can give the other party options under the breach rules.
column4: A breach can never be recognised until the performance due date has passed.

column2: Compensation for legally recoverable loss caused by breach
column3: Remote and unforeseeable losses are distinguished from losses recoverable under the applicable remoteness rules.
column4: Every remotely connected loss is automatically recoverable in full after any breach.

column2: A claim for reasonable remuneration for qualifying work or benefit
column3: In an appropriate non-gratuitous benefit case, reasonable compensation differs from a right to any amount chosen by the claimant.
column4: Quantum meruit always entitles a claimant to an unlimited self-selected fee.

column2: A statutory obligation resembling contractual liability without a true agreement
column3: Returning a qualifying mistaken payment can be required even without a negotiated repayment contract.
column4: No one can owe repayment of a mistaken payment unless a written repayment contract was negotiated beforehand.

column2: A promise to protect another from specified loss
column3: A contract of indemnity is distinguished from a guarantee involving a principal debtor and secondary assurance.
column4: Every indemnity necessarily has the identical three-party debt structure of a guarantee.

column2: An undertaking to answer for another's default under the applicable terms
column3: A guarantee includes creditor principal debtor and surety roles.
column4: A guarantee has no principal-debtor role and is merely a gift to the creditor.

column2: The guarantor's liability under the guarantee and statutory rules
column3: Surety liability is generally co-extensive with the principal debtor's unless the contract provides otherwise.
column4: Surety liability is always unlimited irrespective of the guarantee's agreed terms.

column2: Delivery of possession of goods for a purpose with return or disposal as directed
column3: Giving goods for repair transfers possession for a purpose rather than automatically transferring ownership.
column4: Giving a watch for repair automatically transfers its ownership permanently to the repairer.

column2: Bailment of goods as security for payment or performance
column3: A pledge transfers possession as security, while ownership is not automatically transferred outright to the creditor.
column4: A pledge is necessarily an unconditional outright sale of the goods.

column2: A relationship allowing an agent to act for a principal
column3: An authorised agent's act can bind the principal within the relevant authority.
column4: An agent can bind a principal only if the agent personally owns the principal's entire business.

column2: A principal's valid adoption of an initially unauthorised act
column3: Valid ratification requires the relevant legal conditions and cannot be assumed merely because the principal learns that an act occurred.
column4: Learning about an unauthorised act automatically ratifies it regardless of acceptance and legal conditions.

column2: A goods contract transferring property to the buyer immediately under the contract
column3: An immediate transfer of ownership differs from a future conditional agreement to transfer it.
column4: Every agreement to sell transfers ownership immediately regardless of its stated future condition.

column2: A goods contract where ownership transfer is future or conditional
column3: A future ownership transfer can leave the seller bearing ownership-related consequences until transfer, subject to agreement and law.
column4: Every agreement to sell necessarily transfers all ownership consequences on the signing date.

column2: A stipulation essential to the contract's main purpose
column3: A breach of condition can have stronger remedies than an ordinary warranty breach, subject to rules treating a condition as a warranty.
column4: A condition and warranty necessarily produce identical remedies in every circumstance.

column2: A collateral stipulation whose breach ordinarily supports damages
column3: An ordinary warranty breach generally supports damages rather than automatic rejection of the goods.
column4: Every ordinary warranty breach automatically entitles rejection regardless of statutory conditions.

column2: The buyer-beware principle subject to statutory exceptions
column3: Reliance on the seller's skill for a disclosed purpose can bring an implied fitness obligation under the applicable conditions.
column4: Caveat emptor has no exceptions even when the buyer validly relies on the seller's skill for a disclosed purpose.

column2: A seller meeting the statutory non-payment criteria with specified protective rights
column3: A seller's lien and stoppage in transit have different conditions and are not unlimited rights over goods in every location.
column4: An unpaid seller may seize goods from any person anywhere without regard to ownership transfer or legal conditions.

column2: An instrument transferable with the legal features of negotiability
column3: Negotiation can transfer holder rights in a manner distinct from an ordinary assignment.
column4: Negotiation and assignment necessarily have identical legal effects in every respect.

column2: A written unconditional undertaking to pay a certain sum under the statute
column3: A note contains a promise to pay rather than an order to a third person to pay.
column4: Every promissory note is an order addressed to a bank to pay on demand.

column2: A written unconditional order directing payment under the statute
column3: A bill involves an order by the drawer to the drawee rather than the maker's own promise in a note.
column4: A bill of exchange contains only the maker's own promise and no drawee role.

column2: A bill drawn on a specified banker and payable on demand
column3: A cheque's demand-payment feature distinguishes it from a time bill payable after a stated future period.
column4: Every cheque is necessarily payable only after a fixed future maturity period.

column2: A holder meeting statutory consideration timing and good-faith requirements
column3: Possession alone does not establish all holder-in-due-course requirements.
column4: Anyone physically holding an instrument is automatically a holder in due course regardless of knowledge and consideration.

column2: A company's legal identity distinct from its members
column3: Company property belongs to the company rather than to shareholders as individual owners of each corporate asset.
column4: A shareholder can personally dispose of any company asset merely by owning shares.

column2: Members' liability limited according to the entity and membership terms
column3: Limited shareholder liability does not mean the company itself has no liability for its debts.
column4: Limited shareholder liability automatically cancels the company's debts to outsiders.

column2: The constitutional document containing a company's fundamental charter matters
column3: The memorandum's object framework differs from internal procedural rules principally found in articles.
column4: The memorandum and articles are necessarily the same document with no distinct function.

column2: Rules governing a company's internal administration
column3: Articles operate within applicable company law and the memorandum rather than overriding statutory requirements.
column4: Articles can make every statutory company-law obligation optional.

column2: A formal decision process requiring applicable notice quorum and voting rules
column3: A meeting needs the applicable quorum; a large vote count alone does not cure every procedural defect.
column4: Any decision with many favourable votes is automatically valid despite all notice and quorum defects.

column2: A process for closing affairs and dealing with claims and assets under applicable law
column3: Winding up a company differs from a mere change of shareholders in a continuing company.
column4: Any sale of shares by one shareholder necessarily winds up the company.

column2: A body corporate combining separate personality with a partnership-based structure
column3: An LLP is distinct from an ordinary partnership in its statutory entity status and liability structure.
column4: An LLP is legally identical to an ordinary partnership with no separate entity status.

column2: Law addressing anti-competitive conduct and relevant combinations
column3: Dominance itself is distinguished from abuse of dominance; the legal assessment requires the relevant conduct and market context.
column4: Every dominant market position is automatically unlawful regardless of conduct.

column2: A contract formed through electronic communications subject to applicable law
column3: Electronic form does not remove the need for ordinary contract requirements such as genuine assent and lawful object.
column4: Putting an agreement online automatically makes every unlawful object enforceable.

column2: Indian legislation addressing electronic records and specified cyber matters
column3: Recognition of electronic records is distinct from assuming every electronic signature or message is authentic without verification.
column4: An electronic record's existence conclusively proves the identity and authority of its sender.

column2: A statutory access framework for information held by public authorities with applicable exceptions
column3: RTI concerns public authorities and legally accessible information, not an unconditional right to every private company's every secret.
column4: RTI grants an unrestricted right to every private company's confidential records in all cases.

column2: A legal right protecting a qualifying invention under applicable conditions
column3: A patent protects qualifying inventions rather than every business name used to identify a brand.
column4: Every brand name is automatically protected as a patent merely because it is new.

column2: A sign distinguishing the source of goods or services
column3: A trademark protects source identification rather than granting a monopoly over every underlying technical invention.
column4: Registering a brand name as a trademark automatically patents every manufacturing process used by the brand.

column2: Protection for qualifying original expression rather than ideas alone
column3: Copyright can protect a written explanation's expression without giving ownership of the underlying general idea.
column4: Copyright automatically monopolises every abstract idea expressed in a textbook.

column2: India's shared central and state tax structure for relevant supplies
column3: A qualifying ordinary intra-state supply generally involves CGST and SGST, while a qualifying inter-state supply uses IGST.
column4: Every intra-state supply necessarily attracts only IGST and never CGST or SGST.

column2: Credit for qualifying input tax under applicable GST conditions
column3: Input credit depends on eligibility and statutory conditions rather than arising automatically from every expense.
column4: Every business expense automatically permits unrestricted GST credit irrespective of the nature of the supply.

column2: Taxation linked to the place of consumption through applicable supply rules
column3: Place-of-supply rules matter for allocating tax; the supplier's mailing address alone need not determine every transaction's treatment.
column4: The supplier's mailing address alone conclusively determines place of supply for every goods and services transaction.
